questions.knowledge_point: Finding Missing Constants in First-Order Partial Derivative Expressions
questions.problem:
Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Find the values of $a$ and $b$, if 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =axy-{x}^{2}, \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =y-5b{x}^{2}-7, \\ {f}_{x}(1,2) & =19.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the mixed partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{x}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(axy-{x}^{2}) \\  & =ax-0 \\  & =ax \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{y}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y-5b{x}^{2}-7) \\  & =0-10bx-0 \\  & =-10bx\end{aligned}
$$

Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. Hence, we have the identity

$$
\begin{aligned}ax & =-10bx.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $x,$ we get $b=-\frac{a}{10}.$ 

Now, since ${f}_{x}(1,2)=21$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,2) & =19 \\ a\cdot 2\cdot 1-{1}^{2} & =19 \\ 2a & =20 \\ a & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
b=-\frac{a}{10}=-\frac{10}{10}=-1.
$$

questions.problem:
Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Find the values of $a$ and $b$, if 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =a{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+6xy+2x, \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =b{x}^{3}y+3{x}^{2}+2, \\ {f}_{y}(-1,1) & =3.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the mixed partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{x}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(a{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+6xy+2x) \\  & =2a{x}^{2}y+6x+0 \\  & =2a{x}^{2}y+6x \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{y}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(b{x}^{3}y+3{x}^{2}+2) \\  & =3b{x}^{2}y+6x+0 \\  & =3b{x}^{2}y+6x\end{aligned}
$$

Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. Hence, we have the identity

$$
\begin{aligned}2a{x}^{2}y+6x=3b{x}^{2}y+6x.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of ${x}^{2}y$, we see that $a=\frac{3b}{2}.$ 

Now, since ${f}_{y}(-1,1)=3$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-1,1) & =3 \\ b(-1)^{3}(1)+3(-1)^{2}+2 & =3 \\ -b+3+2 & =3 \\ b & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a=\frac{3b}{2}=3.
$$

questions.problem:
Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Find the values of $a$ and $b$, if 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =axy+{y}^{2}-3, \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =2xy+b{x}^{2}+2y, \\ {f}_{x}(1,-2) & =-7.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the mixed partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{x}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(axy+{y}^{2}-3) \\  & =ax+2y \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{y}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy+b{x}^{2}+2y) \\  & =2y+2bx\end{aligned}
$$

Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. Hence, we have the identity

$$
\begin{aligned}ax+2y=2y+2bx.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $x,$ we see that $a=2b.$

Now, since ${f}_{x}(1,-2)=-7$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,-2) & =-7 \\ a(1)(-2)+(-2)^{2}-3 & =-7 \\ -2a+4-3 & =-7 \\ -2a & =-8 \\ a & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
b=\frac{a}{2}=2.
$$

questions.problem:
Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Find the values of $a$ and $b$, if 

$$
{f}_{x}(x,y)=a{y}^{2}x-3y,\,{f}_{y}(x,y)=2{x}^{2}y+bx.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the mixed partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{x}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(a{y}^{2}x-3y) \\  & =2axy-3 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{y}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}y+bx) \\  & =4xy+b\end{aligned}
$$

Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. Hence, we have the identity

$$
\begin{aligned}2axy-3 & =4xy+b.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $xy$ and constant terms, we see that $a=2$ and $b=-3.$

questions.problem:
Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Find the values of $a$ and $b$, if 

$$
{f}_{x}(x,y)=a{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y+2xy,\,{f}_{y}(x,y)={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y+2b{x}^{2}.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the mixed partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{x}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(a{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y+2xy) \\  & =-a{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y+2x \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{y}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y+2b{x}^{2}) \\  & ={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y+4bx.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. Hence, we have the identity

$$
\begin{aligned}-a{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y+2x={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y+4bx.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $x$ and ${e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y,$ respectively, we see that $b=\frac{1}{2}$ and $a=-1.$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Possible Pairs of First-Order Partial Derivatives
questions.problem:
Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Which of the following pairs could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y)?$

- ${f}_{x}(x,y)={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡({e}^{x})$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡({e}^{x})$
- ${f}_{x}(x,y)=\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=\sqrt{1-y}$
- ${f}_{x}(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+1)$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal, that is, ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y).$ Let's check if this condition is true for each of our pairs of first-order partial derivatives.

- For the first pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡({e}^{x}))=0 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡({e}^{x}))={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡({e}^{x}).\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)\ne {f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the first pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the second pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}})=0 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{1-y})=0.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the second pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the third pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1))=0 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+1))=\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+1).\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)\ne {f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the first pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

questions.problem:
Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Which of the following pairs could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y)?$

- ${f}_{x}(x,y)=2x{y}^{2}-y$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=2{x}^{2}y-2x$
- ${f}_{x}(x,y)=yx{e}^{x}+{y}^{2}$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=(x-1){e}^{x}+2xy$
- ${f}_{x}(x,y)=x-y$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡y}-x$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal, that is, ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y).$ Let's check if this condition is true for each of our pairs of first-order partial derivatives.

- For the first pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x{y}^{2}-y)=4xy-1 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}y-2x)=4xy-2.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)\ne {f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the first pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the second pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(yx{e}^{x}+{y}^{2})=x{e}^{x}+2y \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((x-1){e}^{x}+2xy)=x{e}^{x}+2y.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the second pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the third pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x-y)=-1 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡y}-x)=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$,  the third pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is 'II and III only'.

- ${f}_{x}(x,y)=6{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=6xy$
- ${f}_{x}(x,y)=15{x}^{2}-y$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=8y+x$
- ${f}_{x}(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=-3{y}^{2}$

- For the first pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(6{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2})=6y \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(6xy)=6y.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the first pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the second pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(15{x}^{2}-y)=-1 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(8y+x)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)\ne {f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the second pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the third pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1)=0 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{y}^{2})=0.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$,  the third pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{e}^{2x-{y}^{2}})=-4y{e}^{2x-{y}^{2}} \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2y{e}^{2x+{y}^{2}})=-4y{e}^{2x-{y}^{2}}.\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Which of the following pairs could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y)?$

- ${f}_{x}(x,y)={x}^{2}+5y$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=3{x}^{2}-3y$
- ${f}_{x}(x,y)=-2x{e}^{{y}^{3}-{x}^{2}}$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=3{y}^{2}{e}^{{y}^{3}-{x}^{2}}$
- ${f}_{x}(x,y)=3{x}^{2}y-y{e}^{xy}$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)={x}^{3}-x{e}^{xy}$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal, that is, ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y).$ Let's check if this condition is true for each of our pairs of first-order partial derivatives.

- For the first pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+5y)=5 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}-3y)=6x.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)\ne {f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the first pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the second pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2x{e}^{{y}^{3}-{x}^{2}})=-6x{y}^{2}{e}^{{y}^{3}-{x}^{2}} \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{y}^{2}{e}^{{y}^{3}-{x}^{2}})=-6x{y}^{2}{e}^{{y}^{3}-{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the second pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the third pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}y-y{e}^{xy}) \\  & =3{x}^{2}-({e}^{xy}+xy{e}^{xy}), \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}-x{e}^{xy}) \\  & =3{x}^{2}-({e}^{xy}+xy{e}^{xy}).\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the third pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating Expressions of Partial Derivatives at a Point
questions.problem:
Suppose that a function $f(x,y,z)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ and that

$$
\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}=(x{y}^{2}+2y){e}^{xy}+2{z}^{3},\,\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂z}=6x{z}^{2}.
$$

 

Evaluate the following expression at the point $(1,0,1):$

$$
\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂y∂x}+\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. 

Hence, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂y∂x} & =\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂y∂{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}((x{y}^{2}+2y){e}^{xy}+2{z}^{3}) \\  & =(x{y}^{2}+2y)\cdot x{e}^{xy}+(2xy+2)\cdot {e}^{xy}+0 \\  & =({x}^{2}{y}^{2}+4xy+2){e}^{xy}.\end{aligned}
$$

In addition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂z}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(6x{z}^{2}) \\  & =12xz.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate both partial derivatives at the point $(1,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂y∂x}{|}_{(1,0,1)} & =(0+0+2){e}^{0}=2 \\ \frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}{|}_{(1,0,1)} & =12(1)(1)=12\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂y∂x}{|}_{(1,0,1)}+\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}{|}_{(1,0,1)} & =2+12=14.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating Expressions of Partial Derivatives at a Point
questions.problem:
Evaluate ${f}_{xyy}(2,2,2)$ given that a function $f(x,y,z)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ and that

$$
{f}_{yx}(x,y,z)=2y\sqrt{\frac{{z}^{3}}{x}}+3{z}^{3}\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. 

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xyy}(x,y,z) & ={f}_{yxy}(x,y,z) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{yx}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y\sqrt{\frac{{z}^{3}}{x}}+3{z}^{3}\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}}) \\  & =2\sqrt{\frac{{z}^{3}}{x}}+3{z}^{3}\sqrt{x}(-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{y}^{3}}}) \\  & =2\sqrt{\frac{{z}^{3}}{x}}-\frac{3}{2}{z}^{3}\sqrt{\frac{x}{{y}^{3}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point  $(2,2,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xyy}(2,2,2) & =2\sqrt{\frac{(2)^{3}}{(2)}}-\frac{3}{2}(2)^{3}\sqrt{\frac{(2)}{(2)^{3}}} \\  & =2\cdot 2-3\cdot 2 \\  & =4-6 \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first, second and third-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ What is the value of ${f}_{yxx}(0,3)+{f}_{xx}(0,3)-{f}_{xxy}(0,3)$ given that ${f}_{xx}(x,y)=6-y{e}^{x}?$
questions.worked_solution:
As the function and its first, second, and third-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ we must have ${f}_{yxx}(x,y)={f}_{xxy}(x,y).$ 

Therefore, we can swap the order of the subscripts in the first term. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{yxx}(0,3)+{f}_{xx}(0,3)-{f}_{xxy}(0,3) & ={f}_{yxx}(0,3)+{f}_{xx}(0,3)-{f}_{yxx}(0,3) \\  & =\cancel{{f}_{yxx}(0,3)}+{f}_{xx}(0,3)-\cancel{{f}_{yxx}(0,3)} \\  & ={f}_{xx}(0,3) \\  & =6-(3){e}^{0} \\  & =6-3 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. Hence, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xyx}(x,y) & ={f}_{xxy}(x,y) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{xx}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}{e}^{xy}\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)) \\  & ={x}^{2}(x{e}^{xy}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+{e}^{xy}\cdot (-x\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy))) \\  & ={x}^{3}{e}^{xy}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(\pi ,1):$

$$
{f}_{xyx}(1,\pi )={1}^{3}{e}^{1\cdot \pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡(1\cdot \pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(1\cdot \pi ))=-{e}^{\pi }
$$

questions.problem: Given that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ evaluate ${f}_{yxy}(1,2)$ if ${f}_{yy}(x,y)={x}^{2}{y}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-y).$
questions.worked_solution:
As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. Hence, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{yxy}(x,y) & ={f}_{yyx}(x,y) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{yy}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{y}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-y)) \\  & ={y}^{3}(2x\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-y)+{x}^{2}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x-y)\cdot 2) \\  & =2x{y}^{3}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-y)+x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x-y)).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,2):$

$$
{f}_{xyx}(1,2)=2\cdot 1\cdot {2}^{3}\cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot 1-2)+1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot 1-2))=16.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding Missing Constants in First-Order Partial Derivative Expressions
canonical_examples.problem:
Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Find the values of $a$ and $b,$ if 

$$
f_x(x,y) = 6xy+axy^3-5, \qquad
f_y(x,y) = 3x^2+bx^2y^2, \qquad
f_y(2,-1) = -24.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we compute the mixed partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{x}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(6xy+ax{y}^{3}-5) \\  & =6x+3ax{y}^{2}-0 \\  & =6x+3ax{y}^{2} \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{y}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}+b{x}^{2}{y}^{2}) \\  & =6x+2bx{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. So, we have the identity

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & ={f}_{yx}(x,y) \\ 6x+3ax{y}^{2} & =6x+2bx{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $xy^2,$ we see that $3a=2b.$ 

Now, since $f_y(2,-1)=-24,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(2,-1) & =-24 \\ 3(2)^{2}+b(2)^{2}(-1)^{2} & =-24 \\ 12+4b & =-24 \\ 4b & =-36 \\ b & =-9\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}3a & =2b \\ 3a & =2(-9) \\ 3a & =-18 \\ a & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $a=-6$ and $b=-9.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying Possible Pairs of First-Order Partial Derivatives
canonical_examples.problem:
Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Which of the following pairs could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y)?$

- $f_x(x,y)=x+2y$ and $f_y(x,y)=2y-x$

- $f_x(x,y)=5(x+y)^4$ and $f_y(x,y)=5(x+y)^4$

- $f_x(x,y)=-\sin{x}\sin{y}$ and $f_y(x,y)=\cos{x}\cos{y}$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal, that is,

$$
f_{xy}(x,y)=f_{yx}(x,y).
$$

Let's check if this condition is true for each of our pairs of first-order partial derivatives.

- For the first pair, the mixed partial derivatives are

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+2y)=2, \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y-x)=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f_{xy}(x,y) \neq f_{yx}(x,y),$ the first pair could *not* represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the second pair, the mixed partial derivatives are

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(5(x+y)^{4})=20(x+y)^{3}, \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(5(x+y)^{4})=20(x+y)^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f_{xy}(x,y) = f_{yx}(x,y),$ the second pair *could* represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the third pair, the mixed partial derivatives are

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y, \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f_{xy}(x,y)=f_{yx}(x,y),$  the third pair *could* represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Evaluating Expressions of Partial Derivatives at a Point
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the function $f(x,y,z).$ Given that all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ and that

$$
\dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial z\partial x} = -e^xy\sin{(yz)},
$$

 

evaluate the following expression at the point $(1,\pi,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\dfrac{\partial^3 f}{\partial z\partial x\partial z}+ \dfrac{\partial^3 f }{\partial x \partial z \partial y}
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. 

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z} & =\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂z∂x} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂z∂x}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(-{e}^{x}y\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz)) \\  & =-{e}^{x}{y}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz).\end{aligned}
$$

In addition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂z∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂z∂x}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-{e}^{x}y\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz)) \\  & =-{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz)-{e}^{x}yz\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz) \\  & =-{e}^{x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(yz)+yz\operatorname{cos}⁡(yz)).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate both partial derivatives at the point $(1,\pi,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}{|}_{(1,\pi ,1)} & =-{e}^{(1)}(\pi )^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot 1)=e{\pi }^{2} \\ \frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂z∂y}{|}_{(1,\pi ,1)} & =-{e}^{(1)}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi \cdot 1)+(\pi )(1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot 1))=e\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂z∂x∂z}{|}_{(1,\pi ,1)}+\frac{{∂}^{3}f}{∂x∂z∂y}{|}_{(1,\pi ,1)} & =e{\pi }^{2}+e\pi =e\pi (\pi +1).\end{aligned}
$$
